✋ This robotic hand costs less than $2,000 and can be 3D printed in a single day. It also just ran autonomously for seven hours without a single hardware failure…👀 Researchers at ETH Zurich created ORCA, an open-source tendon-driven hand with tactile sensors on each fingertip, a self-calibration system, and joints designed to dislocate rather than break under stress. Comparable robotic hands with human-like dexterity typically cost over $100,000 and require enterprise-level maintenance. ORCA can hold over 20 pounds and learn manipulation tasks through both imitation learning and simulation-to-real transfer.  All design files and source code are publicly available one their website: orcahand.com and on GitHub - github.com/orcahand

artist and automata maker Amedeo Capelli, known as Stoccafisso Design, creates playful mechanical sculptures from wood, wire and simple mechanisms. In his recent shrimp automata, a handmade crustacean comes to life through a system of wooden gears, cams, rods and rotating parts hidden beneath the stage. Turning the crank transfers motion through the mechanism, making the shrimp’s body and limbs move in an exaggerated, almost theatrical way. Capelli’s work combines traditional automata-making, kinetic sculpture and humor. Instead of hiding the mechanics, he often leaves them visible, allowing us to understand how a simple rotation can be transformed into surprisingly complex movement. #shrimp #art #artist #niche #weird

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

🤖 A Tesla robot showed up to a roofing crew and started hauling bundles up the ladder like it was nothing. And I get why its going around. It looks real. The brand on the bundles is real (IKO Cambridge). The crew on the roof looks real. The robot moves smooth and confident right up the ladder. But I spent years throwing these exact bundles. And something in this video is dead wrong 👇 Watch the shingles. A bundle of shingles weighs 60 to 80 pounds. It is stiff. It is flat. When you carry one it holds its shape or it creases hard. Now look at what the bundles do in this clip. They bend. They curl. They drape over the robots head and shoulders like wet towels 🚩 Shingles do not do that. Ever. That is the tell. This is AI generated video, and the thing that gives it away is not the robot at all. Its the shingles behaving like fabric instead of 70 pounds of asphalt and stone. Real objects keep their weight. AI forgets that heavy things are heavy. A few more once you know: the bundles change shape and count between frames, the robot is carrying over 200 pounds up a ladder (the real Tesla bot handles about 45 and cannot climb ladders at all), and that smooth plastic look is the fingerprint of these video generators 🧠 These robot construction fakes are everywhere right now. Robots roofing, framing, hanging drywall. They go viral because they scare the exact people who do the work. Do not let a three second clip convince you your trade is gone. The robots are coming eventually. But this one? This one is a cartoon with good lighting 🤖❌ If you work a trade, watch the weight. Physics is the one thing AI still cannot fake 🛠️ Save this so you can spot the next one. And send it to the one guy in your crew who already believed it 😂 #roofing #AI #deepfake #tradeslife #tesla

For the past couple of years, @tomasbarcelocastela has been creating robots that combine delicate embossed metal textures with the appearance of old, weathered wood. Wood so aged and cracked that the robots seem to have repaired themselves with staples, rivets, and whatever they could find. When Tomás first started making them, he wasn't entirely sure why. But over time, these details found their place in his personal mythology of Kal's robots. Anat Vel is part of this universe. An anthropomorphic figure inspired by biomechanics, with organic shapes, intricate reliefs, and circular elements suggesting an artificial anatomy. Originally sculpted in fine grog refractory clay, reproduced in resin, and finished with layers of shellac, chalk paint, acrylics, ferric paint, and varnish. And there's something else behind these worn surfaces and carefully repaired bodies: a certain envy these robots feel towards humans. A 2.5 kg box in its arms, wet grass under its feet. HECTOR is a research humanoid developed at the University of Southern California, and its locomotion experiments go well beyond walking on a flat floor. The team tested the robot on wet grass, rough ground, randomly placed wooden slats and stacked boards up to 6 cm high. HECTOR reached 0.6 m/s in the reported walking experiments. It also carried a 2.5 kg load while stepping over uneven terrain. On the wooden slats, a foot can land at a different height or angle. Carrying a box also changes how the robot must balance its body. The researchers used force-and-moment-based model predictive control to calculate the forces and moments applied by the feet. The controller accounts for the robot and the object it carries when planning movement. They also tested balance under external pushes and changes in foot placement. HECTOR is a research platform, and the team released its simulation and control software, including a ROS and Gazebo environment.
